chapters.name: Chapter 1: Choose how you will earn

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Six ways businesses earn with AI
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Describe six real AI earning models and an example of each.
This lesson builds toward: Given the six AI earning models, you will describe each model and give an example that fits your skills or business, for all six models.
1) AI-assisted services: you do work for clients faster with AI, such as social posts, résumés, bookkeeping clean-up. 2) Productized services: a fixed package at a fixed price, such as "10 product descriptions for $X". 3) Digital products: templates, guides, planners or courses you make once and sell many times.
4) Subscriptions: a monthly product or service, such as a weekly content pack or a small AI software tool. 5) Content with sponsors or affiliates: you teach or entertain with AI help and earn from sponsors or affiliate links, with clear disclosure. 6) Cost savings: in an existing business, AI that saves hours or cuts costs is money too.
None of these is automatic income. Each needs real customers, real value and real work. AI mainly lowers the time it takes to make and deliver.
Words to know:
- Monetize: find a way to earn money from something.
- Productized service: a service sold as a fixed package with a fixed price.
- Affiliate link: a link that pays you a commission when someone buys through it.
Try it now: Write the six models with one example of each that could fit your skills or business.
You can now name six real ways to earn with AI and give an example of each.

options: Something made once and sold many times online
A service you do by hand for each client
check.why: Digital products are made once and can be sold again and again.

check.q: You run a bakery and use AI to cut two hours of paperwork each week. Which model is this?
options: Cost savings in an existing business
check.why: Money saved in a business counts as money earned.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Matching a model to your strengths
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Choose the earning model that fits your skills, audience and time.
This lesson builds toward: Given your skills, hours, network and audience, you will choose one earning model to focus on for 90 days, with a written reason it fits what you already have.
The best model depends on what you already have. Skills and time but no audience: services or productized services usually earn fastest. An audience (followers, an email list, a community): digital products, subscriptions or sponsored content may fit. An existing business: start with cost savings and an add-on service for current customers.
Ask AI to help you think it through: "Here are my skills, my time each week, who I know and any audience I have. Compare the six AI earning models for me: speed to first sale, start-up cost, risk and effort." Then decide yourself.
Pick ONE model for the next 90 days. Trying all six at once is the most common reason people earn nothing.
Step by step:
- Write your skills, weekly hours, network and audience.
- Ask AI to compare the six models for you.
- Score each: speed, cost, risk, effort.
- Choose one model for 90 days.
Words to know:
- Audience: people who already follow, read or listen to you.
- Start-up cost: money needed before you can make the first sale.
Try it now: List your skills, hours, network and audience, have AI compare the six models for you, and choose one model for the next 90 days.
You can now choose an AI earning model that fits what you already have.

check.q: How many earning models should you focus on for 90 days?
check.why: Trying everything at once is a common reason people earn nothing.

check.q: You have strong writing skills and time but no audience. What do you choose?
check.why: Services usually earn fastest when you have skills but no audience yet.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Pricing by value
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Set a price based on the value to the customer, checked against your costs.
This lesson builds toward: For your chosen model, you will set a price between your cost floor and the value to the customer, with two competitor prices compared and the math checked in a spreadsheet.
AI makes work faster, which tempts people to charge less. Customers pay for the result, not your minutes. Ask: what does this save or earn the customer? If your listing pack helps a shop sell more, or your template saves a manager two hours a week, the price can reflect that value.
Then check your floor: your costs (tools, fees, time including checking) plus profit. Look at what similar offers charge. Your price should sit between your floor and the value to the customer.
Ask AI for pricing structures (three tiers, bundles, launch price) but set and check the numbers yourself. Keep records for taxes; self-employed people generally pay self-employment tax; see irs.gov or ask an accountant.
Step by step:
- Estimate the value to the customer.
- Work out your floor: costs plus profit.
- Check what similar offers charge.
- Set a price between floor and value.
- Ask AI for structures, then check the numbers.
Words to know:
- Value-based price: a price based on what the result is worth to the customer.
- Price floor: the lowest price that still covers your costs and profit.
- Tier: one level of a product at a set price, like basic or premium.
Official sources:
- IRS: Self-Employed Individuals Tax Center
Try it now: For your chosen model, write the value to the customer, your floor, two competitor prices, and your price. Check the math in a spreadsheet.
You can now price an AI-assisted offer by value, above your costs.

options: The lowest price a competitor charges
check.why: Below the floor, each sale loses money.

check.q: AI says your task takes only five minutes, so you should charge very little. What do you do?
options: Price by the value of the result, above your floor
check.why: Customers pay for the result, not for how long AI took.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Build, test and stay safe

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Making a digital product with AI
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Create a first version of a digital product with AI help and your own expertise.
This lesson builds toward: Using AI help and your own expertise, you will create a first version of a digital product or service package for one problem and one buyer, with every fact checked and no claims you cannot prove.
Good digital products solve one problem for one type of buyer: "A weekly meal-prep planner for shift workers", "20 email templates for home cleaners", "A checklist for opening a food truck in your city". Your experience is what makes it worth buying; AI speeds up the drafting and design.
Steps: outline it with AI, write the key parts with your own knowledge, check every fact, design it in Canva or a document, and test it with two or three buyers before a wider launch.
Copyright matters: the US Copyright Office says purely AI-generated material is not protected, while your own creative work and edits can be. Put real human work into anything you want to own, and never copy someone else's product. If you make claims about results ("lose weight", "earn $1,000"), you must be able to prove them.
Step by step:
- Choose one problem and one buyer.
- Outline the product with AI.
- Write the key parts from your own experience.
- Check facts and design it.
- Test with two or three buyers and improve.
Words to know:
- Digital product: something made once and sold many times online, like a template or guide.
- Copyright: the legal right to control copying of an original creative work.
Official sources:
- US Copyright Office: Part 2 Copyrightability report announcement
- FTC: Advertising and Marketing Basics
Try it now: Make the first version of a small digital product (or the first package of your service) with AI help and your own expertise. Check every fact.
You can now create a digital product that combines your expertise with AI speed.

check.q: What makes a digital product worth buying?
options: It was made fully by AI
It solves one problem for one buyer using real expertise
check.why: Focused products built on real expertise give buyers value.

check.q: AI adds "buyers earn $1,000 a month" to your product page. You have no proof. What do you do?

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Recurring revenue and a small launch
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Design a recurring offer or bundle and run a 30-day launch test.
This lesson builds toward: Given your first product or service, you will design a recurring offer or bundle and a 30-day launch test, with a clear target, a way to track it and any sponsorship disclosed.
Recurring revenue (money that comes in every month) is steadier than one-off sales. Options: a monthly content or template pack, a support plan for service clients, a membership, or a small subscription tool. Bundles (product plus a short call, or three products together) raise the value of each sale.
Run a small launch: tell people who already know you, a community you belong to, or past clients. Use AI to draft the announcement, but make it personal and honest. If you use affiliates or sponsors, disclose them clearly (for example "#ad" at the start).
Set a target for 30 days (for example 5 sales or 3 subscribers), track it, and ask buyers what made them buy and what would make it better.
Step by step:
- Design one recurring offer or bundle.
- Draft an honest launch message with AI and personalize it.
- Share it with people and groups that already know you.
- Disclose any sponsors or affiliates clearly.
- Track your 30-day target and ask buyers for feedback.
Words to know:
- Recurring revenue: income that repeats regularly, like monthly subscriptions.
- Bundle: several products or services sold together.
- Disclosure: clearly telling people about a paid relationship.
Official sources:
- FTC: Endorsement Guides, What People Are Asking
Try it now: Design one recurring offer or bundle, write your launch message, and set a 30-day target with how you will track it.
You can now design recurring income and launch an offer with a clear, measurable test.

options: Income that repeats, such as a monthly subscription
check.why: Recurring offers bring income every month.

check.q: A brand pays you to mention its AI tool in your newsletter. What do you do?
options: Disclose it clearly, such as "#ad" at the start
Mention it only at the very end in small print
check.why: Sponsored content must be clearly disclosed.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Spotting AI money-making scams
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use a red-flag checklist before paying for any AI income program or coaching.
This lesson builds toward: Before paying for any AI income program or coaching, you will check it against a written red-flag checklist, asking for the disclosure document and knowing where to report a scam.
Many programs sell "AI income": done-for-you online stores, AI trading bots, "passive income" courses. The FTC has taken action against several. In one case it described, a company promised to use AI to pick top-selling products for online stores, but the FTC charged that its earnings claims were baseless and most clients did not get back what they paid.
FTC advice before buying a business or coaching opportunity: ask for the legally required one-page disclosure document; check it names the seller and any lawsuits; read the cancellation and refund terms; ask for references; if they claim you can earn money, get the earnings claim statement; and walk away if what they say does not match their documents.
Other red flags: guaranteed income, pressure to buy today, big upfront fees, vague "secret AI", and contracts that stop you leaving honest reviews. Report suspected scams at ReportFraud.ftc.gov. This course does not recommend any investment or trading product.
Step by step:
- Ask for the one-page disclosure document.
- Check the seller's name and lawsuits.
- Read refund and cancellation terms.
- Ask for references and the earnings claim statement.
- Walk away if anything does not match; report scams at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.
Words to know:
- Business opportunity: a program sold as a ready-made way to start earning.
- Earnings claim: a statement about how much money you could make.
- Red flag: a warning sign of a scam.
Official sources:
- FTC Consumer Alert: Vetting a business or coaching opportunity before you buy in
Try it now: Final task: write your red-flag checklist, then put together your monetization plan: model and why, priced offer, first product or recurring offer, and 30-day launch test.
You can now earn with AI through honest, tested offers and avoid AI money-making scams.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Model and why No model chosen, or several at once. One model with a written reason it fits the learner's skills, time and audience. Also says which models were ruled out and why. Value-based price Price below the cost floor, or no math. Price between the floor and the value, with two competitor prices and checked math. Explains the value in the customer's terms. First product or offer Unchecked AI content, or claims that cannot be proven. A first version for one problem and one buyer, facts checked, with the learner's own expertise. Shown to at least one possible buyer for feedback. Launch test No target or no way to track it. A 30-day test with a clear target, a launch message and tracking. Includes a recurring offer or bundle and disclosure for any sponsorship. Red-flag checklist No checklist, or it misses guaranteed income or pressure tactics. A checklist covering guarantees, pressure, upfront fees and the disclosure document. Notes where to report a suspected scam. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: Which is a red flag in an AI income program?
options: A free trial with no promises
Clear prices and a refund policy
Guaranteed earnings and pressure to pay today
check.why: Guaranteed income and pressure to buy now are warning signs.

check.q: A coach wants a big upfront fee for an "AI store" business opportunity. What do you do first?
options: Pay quickly before the price rises
Ask for the one-page disclosure document and check your red-flag list
check.why: Ask for the disclosure document and check red flags before paying.
